<reason>Both sides built genuinely strong cases, but PRO (B) controlled the decisive clash. CON's best material — legitimacy does not detect error, the correction mechanism is parasitic on expertise, most conflicts are empirical — was met squarely: B never claimed voters detect error, expertise detects while legitimacy supplies the power to act and the "reason to look" (Flint), and the delegation/accountant structure showed authority writing the terms rather than signing a confession. CON's mill-town answer ("no expert method — and no democratic method either") dodged B's actual question of who is authorized to choose, and CON's chef/menu metaphor was cleanly reversed ("the chef does not own the restaurant"). B's closing advice-vs-authority crystallization matched the motion's comparative ("strip legitimacy and analysis becomes a memo; strip competence and you still have a government you can throw out") and directly answered CON's consequences-over-pedigree frame. CON's closing was sharp but slightly overreached ("signing whatever is put in front of him"). Execution costs: CON's Rebuttal 2 was clipped mid-weighing, and B once misdescribed CON as "twice declining" a question CON had in fact answered. On balance, B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over CON's chef/menu metaphor: CON argued the selector choosing from an expert-written menu cannot outrank the chef, and PRO's reply — the chef writes the menu but does not own the restaurant, and the meal is not cooked for his sake — reversed CON's own image while tying it to the ends/means structure that decided the motion.</best_rebuttal>
